opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm optimistic because we've already watched this movie play out once, with language. A few years ago, NLP was a zoo of task-specific models: one for translation, one for sentiment, one for summarization. Then we found a simple recipe. Take a transformer, feed it an enormous amount of data, scale up the compute, and generalist capabilities emerge that nobody explicitly programmed. I don't see a fundamental reason why that recipe stops working when the output is motor actions instead of text tokens.

The transformer is agnostic about what it's modeling. Text, pixels, joint angles, force readings: once you tokenize them, it's all sequences. So the architecture isn't the bottleneck. The real bottleneck in robotics has always been data. With language models we had the internet, which is basically a fossil fuel of human text. Robotics has no internet of motor control. You can't scrape torque data from Wikipedia.

That's where I get excited, because I think we can manufacture that data. I think of it in three layers. First, internet-scale video and text, which give the model common sense about how the world looks and how humans behave. Second, simulation. With GPU-accelerated physics we can run thousands of simulated robots in parallel, ten thousand times faster than real time, and generate effectively unlimited trajectories. Increasingly, generative models can also create the simulated worlds themselves. Third, real-world data from teleoperation, which is expensive and limited but grounds everything in reality. Mix those properly and you get a data pyramid that can actually feed a scaling curve.

Then there's transfer. A foundation model trained across many embodiments, tasks, and environments should pick up something more general than any single robot policy, the same way GPT picked up reasoning it was never directly trained on. We're starting to see early signs of that. Policies get more robust as you add diverse data, and skills carry over between different robot bodies.

I don't want to oversell it. Robotics is harder than language in some ways. Physics doesn't forgive mistakes, latency matters, and the long tail of real-world situations is brutal. But the trend lines look the way language looked before its breakthrough. My bet is that within a few years we'll have our "GPT moment" for robotics, a single generalist model that can be prompted to do a wide range of physical tasks. And I think the path there runs straight through scaling.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data volume and sources, but does not identify training-token quality as a determinant of transformer model quality.

r002.rationale: It proposes a data strategy combining internet-scale video and text, simulation trajectories, and real-world teleoperation data.

r003.rationale: It connects scaling data and compute with emergent generalist capabilities, but does not clearly identify high-quality embodied training data as part of that joint scaling hypothesis.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that I've watched the same architecture eat one modality after another, and I don't see a principled reason why the body is the exception.

Look at what happened with language. Nobody hand-engineered grammar into GPT. You took a general sequence model, fed it an enormous amount of data, and syntax, reasoning, even some world knowledge fell out as a byproduct of predicting the next token. Then the same recipe worked on images, on video, on audio, on protein sequences. Every time someone said "this domain is special, you need domain-specific inductive biases," scale and data eventually won.

Robotics has been the holdout, and I think the reason is mostly that the data was never there, not that transformers are the wrong tool. Language had the internet. Vision had the internet. A robot arm picking up a cup has maybe a few thousand demonstrations collected in one lab in one lighting condition. Of course that doesn't generalize. But that's a data problem, not an architecture problem.

What makes me optimistic right now is that the data problem is finally becoming tractable from several directions at once. Simulation is one. With GPU-accelerated physics you can run thousands of environments in parallel and generate years of experience in hours. Then you layer on domain randomization and generative models to make the sim diverse enough that the real world looks like just another sample. Video is another. There are billions of hours of humans doing things with their hands online, and a transformer trained on that is learning something about how objects respond to contact and how tasks decompose, even before it ever controls a motor. And then the pretrained foundation models themselves become a lever. If a vision-language model already understands what a kitchen is and what "put the dishes away" means, the robot policy doesn't have to learn that from scratch. It only has to learn the last mile of mapping intent to actuation.

The other thing I'd point to is that a transformer is just a very good general-purpose function approximator over sequences, and a robot is a sequence problem. Observations in, actions out, over time. Whether the tokens are words, pixels, or joint angles doesn't fundamentally change the machinery. We've already seen early evidence of positive transfer, where training one model across many robot embodiments makes each individual robot better. That's the same cross-task transfer we saw in language, showing up in a physical setting.

I'll be honest that embodiment has real differences. You can't reset the physical world, actions have consequences, data is expensive, and you need to run at real-time latency. Those are hard engineering constraints. But I think of them as friction on the curve, not a wall. My bet is that we'll get a foundation model for robotics the same way we got one for language: one big model, lots of diverse data, and the behaviors we currently handcraft will emerge on their own.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics lacks enough data, but does not identify training-token quality as a determinant of model quality.

r002.rationale: It discusses internet video and simulation as data sources, but does not propose combining them with real robot data as a training strategy; real robot demonstrations are mentioned as scarce.

r003.rationale: It predicts behaviors may emerge from a big model trained on diverse data, but does not clearly hypothesize jointly scaling model size and high-quality embodied training data.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic because we’ve seen that one architecture can learn very different kinds of structure. With language, it learns relationships between words and concepts. With images and video, it learns spatial and temporal patterns. In embodied AI, the question is whether we can extend that to actions: given what I see and what I want to accomplish, what should I do next?

But I don’t think the recipe is simply to make a language model bigger and attach it to a robot. The data matters enormously. The internet contains a lot of descriptions of the world, but much less experience of acting in it—the consequences of pushing something, losing your balance, or failing to grasp an object. You need that feedback.

That’s why simulation is so exciting. It gives us a way to generate experience at scale, across different environments, objects, and tasks. Then the challenge is to make what the model learns transfer to the real world.

So my optimism is about combining a scalable learning architecture with a scalable source of interaction. We still have hard problems to solve, but there’s a plausible path toward a model that can reuse what it learns across many physical tasks, rather than starting over for each one.

r001.rationale: The response says data matters, but it does not identify training-token quality as a determinant of transformer model quality.

r002.rationale: It describes internet descriptions and simulated experience, but does not propose combining them with real robot data as a training strategy.

r003.rationale: It suggests scalable architecture plus scalable interaction could enable reuse across physical tasks, but does not hypothesize joint scaling of high-quality embodied data and model size producing emergent capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic because a transformer is a very general way to learn patterns across sequences. Those sequences can be words, but they can also be images, observations, and actions. For an embodied agent, the question becomes: given what I’ve seen and what I’m trying to accomplish, what should I do next?

The big challenge is data. On the internet, we have an enormous amount of text. We don’t have an equivalent amount of robot experience. Physical robots are slow to collect data with, and failures can be expensive. That’s why simulation is so exciting: you can run many environments in parallel, vary the conditions, and give agents opportunities to learn through interaction.

I don’t think scaling means simply making a language model bigger and attaching it to a robot. We need to scale experience, the diversity of tasks, and the quality of feedback. But transformers give us a promising architecture for bringing those things together. If we can build that learning loop, I think we have a real path toward agents that generalize beyond the specific tasks they were trained on.

r001.rationale: It discusses scaling experience, task diversity, and feedback, but does not identify training-token quality as a determinant of transformer model quality.

r002.rationale: It mentions internet text, simulation, and the scarcity of robot experience, but does not propose combining internet, simulation, and real-robot data as a training strategy.

r003.rationale: It advocates scaling experience and task diversity, but does not hypothesize that jointly scaling high-quality embodied data and model size will produce emergent capabilities.
